| $f(x)$ | $0.5$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |

Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{50}$ be a random sample of size $n=50$ from a population with the probability mass function given above. Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is greater than $2.2.$

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =50,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =1\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.2+3\cdot 0.1+4\cdot 0.2 \\  & =0.5+0.4+0.3+0.8 \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =({1}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.2+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.2)-{2}^{2} \\  & =(0.5+0.8+0.9+3.2)-4 \\  & =1.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(2,\frac{1.4}{50}) \\  & ∼N(2,0.028).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>2.2).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>2.2) & ≈P(Z>\frac{2.2-2}{\sqrt{0.028}}) \\  & =P(Z>1.20) \\  & =1-Φ(1.20).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(\overset{―}{X}>2.2)=1-Φ(1.20).
$$

Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =50,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }x\cdot \frac{5}{{x}^{6}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{5}{{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}\frac{5}{{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{[-\frac{5}{4{x}^{4}}]}_{1}^{b} \\  & =\frac{5}{4} \\  & =1.25,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.1.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(1.25,\frac{0.1}{50}) \\  & ∼N(1.25,0.002).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<1.2).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<1.2) & =P(Z<\frac{1.2-1.25}{\sqrt{0.002}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-1.12) \\  & =Φ(-1.12)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have that

$$
Φ(-1.12)=0.1314.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<1.2) & =Φ(-1.12) \\  & =0.1314.\end{aligned}
$$

f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{x}^{3}, & 0\le x\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the population variance ${\sigma }^{2}=0.11,$ calculate $P(1.6<\overset{―}{X}<1.7).$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =55,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{1}{4}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{5}}{20}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{32}{20} \\  & =1.6,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.11.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(1.6,\frac{0.11}{55}) \\  & ∼N(1.6,0.002).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(1.6<\overset{―}{X}<1.7).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1.6<\overset{―}{X}<1.7) & =P(\frac{1.6-1.6}{\sqrt{0.002}}<Z<\frac{1.7-1.6}{\sqrt{0.002}}) \\  & ≈P(0<Z<2.24) \\  & =P(Z<2.24)-P(Z<0) \\  & =Φ(2.24)-Φ(0)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(2.24)=0.9875,
$$

and by the symmetry of the normal distribution, $Φ(0)=0.5.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1.6<\overset{―}{X}<1.7) & =Φ(2.24)-Φ(0) \\  & =0.9875-0.5 \\  & =0.4875.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =30,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot 4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{4{x}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{5} \\  & =0.8,\end{aligned}

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(0.8,\frac{0.03}{30}) \\  & ∼N(0.8,0.001).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7) & =P(Z>\frac{0.7-0.8}{\sqrt{0.001}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>-3.16)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the complement of the normal distribution, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>-3.16) & =1-P(Z<-3.16) \\  & =1-Φ(-3.16).\end{aligned}

From the table, we have that

$$
Φ(-3.16)=0.0008.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7) & =1-Φ(-3.16) \\  & =1-0.0008 \\  & =0.9992.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3.6<\overset{―}{X}<4.2) & ≈-P(\frac{3.6-4}{\sqrt{0.0625}}<Z<\frac{4.2-4}{\sqrt{0.0625}}) \\  & ≈-P(-1.6<Z<0.8) \\  & =P(Z<0.8)-P(Z<-1.6) \\  & =Φ(0.8)-Φ(-1.6).\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.8)=0.7881, \\ Φ(-1.6)=0.0548.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3.6<\overset{―}{X}<4.2) & =Φ(0.8)-Φ(-1.6) \\  & =0.7881-0.0548 \\  & =0.7333.\end{aligned}
